items.prompt: What does 'tribal knowledge' mean?
choices: Context the team depends on that lives only in people's heads
A formal document that every new hire signs on day one for the whole project
Knowledge shared openly in a well-kept internal wiki
items.explanation: It is exactly the context that was never written anywhere searchable.

items.prompt: In the opening story, why did Jordan raise the retry count?
choices: The code gave no sign the number was deliberate
Jordan ignored a clear warning in the README
The retry count was already marked as outdated whatever the circumstances
items.explanation: Nothing in the code, README, or PR explained the value, so it looked arbitrary.

items.prompt: Who was at fault for Jordan's near-miss?
choices: Nobody individually; the reason was never recorded
Jordan, for not reading the code carefully enough
The reviewer, for catching it so late in the process
items.explanation: The failure was in where the decision lived, not in Jordan's effort.

items.prompt: Where did the reason for the retry cap live?
choices: In a past meeting and one departed engineer's memory
In the project README under a design heading
In a comment on the exact line of code from that point onward
items.explanation: It was made in a meeting with no notes by someone who has since left.

items.prompt: When is tribal knowledge most dangerous?
choices: When the one person who holds it is unreachable
When several people hold the same knowledge from that point onward
When it is also recorded in a decision log
items.explanation: A single holder is a single point of failure.

items.prompt: A newcomer sees an odd constant with no comment. What is the most reasonable assumption without further context?
choices: It may be arbitrary, since nothing says otherwise
It must be critical, since every constant is critical
It is surely documented somewhere they will find it
items.explanation: With no signal, a good-faith reader treats it as tunable; that is the hazard.

items.prompt: Which statement about tribal knowledge is accurate?
choices: Fast-moving teams naturally accumulate some of it
Only badly managed teams ever have any of it
It disappears on its own once a team is big enough
items.explanation: It builds up whenever people decide faster than they record.

items.prompt: Why does the holder leaving matter more than the holder being wrong?
choices: The reason disappears and nobody knows to ask
Departing people always take their code with them
Wrong decisions are always caught during review
items.explanation: The loss is the invisible reason, not the code itself.

items.prompt: Two engineers both know why a legacy timeout is set to 30 seconds. One transfers teams, the other goes on long leave, and a third engineer wants to shorten it. What is the underlying risk?
choices: The reason exists but nobody reachable can supply it
Shortening timeouts is always unsafe in legacy code
Two people knowing it makes the knowledge documented
The third engineer lacks permission to edit the value
items.explanation: Two holders is still tribal knowledge; the risk is that neither is reachable when it matters.
items.reference:
Tribal knowledge
🧠 decision held only in someone's memory
🚪 holder leaves, forgets, or is asleep
⚠️ newcomer guesses in good faith
Why: knowledge nobody can search for is only as durable as the person holding it.
items.learnMore:
Knowledge with a single point of failure

Tribal knowledge is context the team relies on but that exists only in people's heads. It works fine until the holder is unreachable at the moment someone needs it, and then a reasonable newcomer fills the gap with a guess.

Common mistake

Treating tribal knowledge as a sign of a careless team. Every fast team accumulates some; the issue is leaving the important parts unrecorded.
items.reflection: Think of a family recipe that only one relative knows by feel. What happens to it, and to the next cook, when that relative is no longer around?

items.prompt: A team keeps strong code reviews and has a great culture, but its important decisions are made in hallway chats. Which claim best describes it?
choices: Strong reviews make the hallway decisions effectively documented
Hallway decisions are safe as long as everyone is friendly
The team has no tribal knowledge because it communicates well
Good reviews cannot catch constraints that were never recorded
items.explanation: A review catches what a reviewer happens to remember; it does not turn memory into a searchable record.

A server crashes because of a hardware fault whatever the circumstances

Two reviewers disagree about code formatting from that point onward

items.prompt: What is an ADR?
choices: A running log of every code change in a project
A short permanent record of one decision and its reasons
A weekly status report sent to management from that point onward
items.explanation: An Architecture Decision Record captures one decision, why, alternatives, and consequences.

items.prompt: Which place is lost entirely once a meeting ends with no notes?
choices: The meeting itself, as a source of the decision
The code that implements the decision from that point onward
The ADR that records the decision for every later reader
The git history of the repository in practice
items.explanation: With no notes the meeting leaves only memory behind.

items.prompt: What is the main weakness of a chat thread as a record?
choices: Chat messages can never be read by others
Chat threads cannot mention the reason
Threads are always deleted the same day
You must already know to search for it
items.explanation: Chat is searchable only by someone who knows what to look for.

items.prompt: A code comment is strongest when?
choices: The reader is reviewing a graph on a dashboard
The reader is already looking at that exact line
The decision affects many unrelated files at once
items.explanation: Comments have reach only at their own call site.

items.prompt: What does an ADR usually include that a comment rarely does?
choices: The author's favorite coding style notes
The alternatives considered and why each lost
A full copy of the source code involved for the whole project
items.explanation: Recording the rejected options is its core purpose.

items.prompt: How is an ADR organized so a newcomer can find it?
choices: Stored inside each source file it affects
Listed by decision, not by file path
Sorted by the author's name alone
items.explanation: Indexing by decision lets people find it without knowing the code layout.

items.prompt: What happens to an ADR when its decision is later changed?
choices: It is deleted so nobody is confused
A newer ADR replaces it and links back
It is silently rewritten with the new decision
items.explanation: Old records stay; they get superseded.

items.prompt: Why would a comment alone not have fully protected the retry logic?
choices: Comments are ignored by the compiler entirely as a general rule
A second retry call site elsewhere would have no comment
Comments cannot contain numbers or reasons without further review
items.explanation: A comment covers only the place where it sits.

items.prompt: A team records every decision as a comment beside the relevant code. Months later someone adds a second retry loop in another module. What gap does that expose?
choices: Comments are removed automatically during every build whatever the circumstances
The new location has no comment, so the reason is invisible there
The first comment now contradicts the second loop from that point onward
Comments cannot describe retry behavior accurately for every later reader
items.explanation: Comments are tied to one location, so reach stops at that line.
items.reference:
Where a decision lives
📝 meeting: lost
💬 chat thread: hard to find
💡 code comment: one call site
📄 ADR: indexed per decision
Why: a record has to be findable by someone who does not yet know where to look.
items.learnMore:
Reach, not just existence

A decision can exist in a meeting, a chat thread, a comment, or a record. What separates them is whether a newcomer can find it without already knowing the answer, and whether it explains the alternatives that lost.

Common mistake

Picking the fastest place to write instead of the place a future reader will search.
items.reflection: Where do you keep the important facts about your own life, such as a warranty or a medical history, so that someone else could find them in an emergency?

items.prompt: An incident reviewer, looking at a latency graph and not the code, asks why a limit was chosen. Which record is most likely to answer?
choices: An ADR indexed by decision
A comment on the line that sets the limit
The author's memory of the meeting
A chat message from last quarter
items.explanation: The reviewer does not know which file to open, so only a decision-indexed record is reachable.

Comment: local and short; ADR: findable and explains alternatives
items.explanation: The strengths differ in reach and in how much reasoning each carries.

items.prompt: What is documentation culture, in this unit?
choices: Writing as many pages as possible about everything
Reviewing the wiki once a year for typos
Recording costly decisions when they are made
items.explanation: It is a narrow habit, not a volume target.

items.prompt: Why can a wiki nobody updates be worse than none?
choices: Wikis slow down the computers that open them
Empty wikis are easier for newcomers to search
Stale pages are trusted and mislead readers
items.explanation: A confident, out-of-date page causes mistakes.

items.prompt: Which decision is worth a record?
choices: The name of a local loop variable in most teams
The order of imports in one file for the whole project
A data model choice that is hard to reverse
items.explanation: Hard-to-reverse choices are the expensive ones to get wrong.

items.prompt: When is the best time to write the record?
choices: Right before the next release
After the person who decided has left
When the decision is made
items.explanation: Memory and context are freshest at decision time.

items.prompt: A constraint is invisible in the code. Should it be recorded?
choices: No, because the code is the only truth as a general rule
Only if someone asks for it later on whatever the circumstances
Yes, because the code cannot tell the reader
items.explanation: Anything the code cannot reveal needs a separate home.

items.prompt: Which choice does NOT need a record?
choices: A choice about how payments are retried
A rejected design people keep re-proposing without further review
A formatting rule the linter already enforces
items.explanation: Enforced style is already self-documenting.

items.prompt: What does recording rejected ideas prevent?
choices: Any future change to the system without further review
Newcomers reading the existing code
The same debate being rerun from scratch
items.explanation: It saves the team from repeating the argument.

items.prompt: What is the risk of writing a record for every minor choice?
choices: The team runs out of paper to print on
Nothing, since more records are always better
The index becomes noise and stops being read
items.explanation: Signal drowns when everything is equally weighted.

items.prompt: A team proposes: 'every pull request must link a decision record, no exceptions.' What is the most likely outcome?
choices: Every important decision is now guaranteed to be recorded
Review speed improves because decisions are explicit
Most records are trivial and the index stops being useful
Nothing changes, since nobody reads records anyway
items.explanation: Mandating volume drowns the few decisions that matter.
items.reference:
The narrow habit
✅ hard to reverse
✅ invisible in the code
✅ people keep re-proposing it
❌ trivial, reversible, or obvious
Why: a record is worth its upkeep only when a decision is expensive to get wrong twice.
items.learnMore:
Document selectively, at decision time

Documentation culture is not volume. Records for trivial choices bury the important ones, and stale pages mislead. The habit is to record decisions that are costly to repeat, when they are made, where future readers will look.

Common mistake

Writing a record for every small choice and then neglecting the index.
items.reflection: If you could leave only five notes for whoever takes over your responsibilities, which decisions would you choose, and what would you leave out?

items.prompt: Which pair of decisions should most clearly get a record?
choices: Renaming a private helper, and moving a blank line in practice as a general rule
Switching how money movement is retried, and a choice to drop a rejected rewrite
Picking a loop style, and choosing tab width for the whole project without further review
Naming a test file, and trimming a comment as a general rule from that point onward
items.explanation: Both entries are costly to repeat and hard to see from code.

items.prompt: What does 'proposed' mean for an ADR?
choices: The decision is already in force for the whole project
The decision has been replaced as a general rule
The decision was turned down whatever the circumstances
The decision is still under discussion
items.explanation: Proposed means a draft, not how the system behaves yet.

items.prompt: What does 'accepted' mean?
choices: The idea was considered and declined
The record is only a rough draft whatever the circumstances
This is how the system currently works
A newer record has taken over from that point onward
items.explanation: Accepted records are the current, load-bearing decisions.

items.prompt: What happens to a rejected ADR?
choices: It is deleted to reduce clutter whatever the circumstances
It stays in the record with its reasons
It is renamed as accepted later from that point onward
It is merged into the code for every later reader
items.explanation: Rejected records preserve why the idea lost.

items.prompt: What does 'superseded' mean?
choices: Once current, now replaced by a newer record
Never reviewed by anyone on the team from that point onward
Currently being proposed for the first time
Rejected before anyone discussed it in practice
items.explanation: Superseded decisions were real and are now replaced.

items.prompt: Who benefits from reading a rejected ADR?
choices: Someone tempted to re-propose the same idea
Only the person who wrote it originally
Nobody, once the decision is final in practice as a general rule
items.explanation: It prevents the same debate being rerun.

items.prompt: Does an accepted ADR ever stay forever?
choices: No, a later change can supersede it
Yes, accepted records can never be replaced
Only if the author remains on the team
items.explanation: Decisions can be revisited; the record then moves to superseded.

items.prompt: Which state would a reviewer be reading about when deciding whether to approve?
choices: Superseded
Proposed
Rejected
Accepted
items.explanation: Reviewers decide on proposals.

items.prompt: Why does every record show a status and a date?
choices: So a reader knows if it is current or historical
So the file appears sorted alphabetically for the whole project
So the author can claim credit for it as a general rule
items.explanation: Without status and date, a reader cannot judge currency.

items.prompt: An engineer finds ADR-007, status Superseded, in a search and starts following its advice. What should they do first?
choices: Treat it as current since it is in the index for the whole project
Delete it to avoid confusing the next reader as a general rule
Ask the original author whether it still holds whatever the circumstances
Follow the link forward to the record that replaced it
items.explanation: A superseded record is history; its link forward leads to the current decision.
items.reference:
The ADR lifecycle
🟡 proposed: under discussion
🟢 accepted: how the system works
🔴 rejected: kept, with why
⚪ superseded: replaced, links forward
Why: a reader must tell from the record alone whether it is current, turned down, or replaced.
items.learnMore:
Four states a reader can trust

Proposed means still being discussed, accepted means current, rejected means considered and declined, superseded means once current and now replaced. No state is deleted; each tells a reader how much weight to give the page.

Common mistake

Deleting rejected proposals and thereby losing the reason the idea failed.
items.reflection: Think of a library keeping withdrawn editions of a reference book. Why might the old edition still be useful to someone?

items.prompt: A proposal to adopt a new queue is declined in review, and someone wants to delete the draft to keep the index tidy. What is the best response?
choices: Delete it since declined ideas have no value as a general rule
Mark it accepted so the index stays consistent
Keep it marked rejected with the reasons recorded
Move it to the author's personal notes from that point onward
items.explanation: The rejection is the information that spares the next person from re-deriving it.

items.prompt: Which sequence of states is NOT a valid path for a record?
choices: Proposed, then accepted, then superseded whatever the circumstances
Rejected, then later accepted without a new record
Proposed, then rejected from that point onward in most teams
Proposed, then accepted for every later reader
items.explanation: A rejected decision that changes should become a new proposal, not a silent state flip that hides the history.

choices: Context
Consequences
Alternatives
Status

items.prompt: Which section states what was actually chosen?
choices: Context
Alternatives
Date
Decision

items.prompt: What does the alternatives section show?
choices: The author's full employment history
The code diff of the final change in practice as a general rule
Other options considered and why each lost
A list of people who attended for the whole project
items.explanation: It prevents rejected ideas being proposed again.

items.prompt: What does the consequences section show?
choices: Who approved the decision originally in practice
What the decision costs, risks, or rules out
The names of all future maintainers for the whole project
The date the file was last printed as a general rule
items.explanation: Consequences make the price of the decision visible.

items.prompt: What goes wrong if the status and date are missing?
choices: A reader cannot tell if the record is current
The file refuses to open in editors for the whole project
The decision is automatically reversed
Nothing, they are decorative only whatever the circumstances
items.explanation: Currency is the point of those fields.

items.prompt: Must a useful record be long?
choices: Yes, at least several pages are required
Yes, otherwise reviewers ignore it as a general rule
Only when the decision is expensive whatever the circumstances
No, it must answer a reader's real questions
items.explanation: Length is not the measure; coverage of the five questions is.

items.prompt: Which omission makes a decision look free?
choices: Date as a general rule
Context whatever the circumstances
Consequences
Status from that point onward
items.explanation: Without consequences, nothing visibly costs anything.

items.prompt: Which section helps a reader judge whether the decision still applies?
choices: Decision
Context
Status only
Author name
items.explanation: If the situation behind the decision has changed, the context shows it.

items.prompt: A record says only: 'Decision: retries capped at 3.' Which missing sections would most have helped Jordan avoid the near-miss?
choices: Context and consequences
Date and author
Alternatives and file path
Only the status line
items.explanation: Context says why 3 and consequences say that raising it reopens the problem.
items.reference:
What a record needs
📌 context: the forcing situation
✔️ decision: stated as fact
🔀 alternatives: why each lost
💰 consequences: what it costs
🗓️ status and date
Why: each section answers a question a future reader will actually ask.
items.learnMore:
Five sections, each with a job

Context says why the decision was needed, the decision states what was chosen, alternatives show what lost, consequences show the price, and status and date show whether it is current. A short record with all five beats a long one missing one.

Common mistake

Recording only the decision and leaving out its cost, so it reads as free.
items.reflection: Next time you accept a job offer or sign a lease, which of these five pieces would you want written down for your future self?

A previously rejected idea may be proposed as if new
items.explanation: Without alternatives, the effort behind the rejected options is lost.

items.prompt: What should happen when a team changes an accepted decision?
choices: The old record is edited to match the new
A new record supersedes the old one
The old record is deleted outright
Nothing, accepted means final
items.explanation: Changes are made by superseding.

items.prompt: What does the old record get when it is superseded?
choices: A status change and a link to the new record
A new number and a fresh date for the whole project
Its content replaced with the new decision
A note telling readers to ignore it whatever the circumstances
items.explanation: It stays, marked, and points forward.

items.prompt: What does the new record's context explain?
choices: Only the final choice without history for the whole project without further review
The author's reasons for leaving as a general rule
A list of unrelated technical terms whatever the circumstances
What the earlier record decided and why it no longer holds
items.explanation: It connects the new decision to its predecessor.

items.prompt: Why not simply edit the old record?
choices: Edits are impossible in a repository
The old record is read-only by law whatever the circumstances
Editing erases what was decided and when
Editing makes the file too long from that point onward
items.explanation: A record is trustworthy as a statement of past decisions.

items.prompt: An old code comment says 'see ADR-004'. If ADR-004 is edited in place, what is the result?
choices: Nothing changes, the link still works well whatever the circumstances
The comment points at text that no longer justifies the code
The comment is automatically updated from that point onward
The code stops compiling for every later reader for the whole project
items.explanation: The trail between code and its original reasoning is cut.

items.prompt: What does superseding cost?
choices: One additional document and number
The loss of all earlier history from that point onward
A full rewrite of the codebase
The approval of the whole company
items.explanation: It is cheap compared with losing trust in the record.

items.prompt: What can a reader do from an old record link after superseding?
choices: Only see an error page from that point onward
Read the old text with no pointer for every later reader
Delete the old record themselves
Click through to the current answer
items.explanation: The forward link keeps the trail intact.

items.prompt: What does superseding preserve that editing destroys?
choices: The file's original line count for every later reader
The author's spelling mistakes in practice
The record that the earlier choice was deliberate
The record's position in the folder for the whole project
items.explanation: The earlier reasoning remains available for judging future calls.

items.prompt: A team switches from polling to webhooks. A manager suggests changing ADR-004's text, 'to keep things simple'. Which cost of that suggestion is easiest to overlook?
choices: The new text will be longer than before in practice as a general rule
The record that polling was ever a considered choice disappears
The file's date will look unusual in the index for the whole project

items.reference:
Habits that defeat the record
📎 decision buried in a PR description
🕸️ stale, never revisited
🔗 no link from the code
🌊 everything documented equally
🚑 only after incidents
Why: a record that is unfindable, stale, or drowned in noise fails like no record.
items.learnMore:
Looks like documentation, works like none

Several habits resemble documentation but fail one test: findable, current, or worth the click. Linking from the code, revisiting records when the system changes, and being selective are what keep the habit alive.

Common mistake

Counting the number of records as a measure of a healthy documentation culture.
